stops.title: The question
stops.text: This is the last of our three language model foundations, and the one most directly usable in the LTX-2.3 study. AWQ asks how to push a large language model's weights down to four or even three bits, with no retraining and almost no accuracy loss. Activations stay in sixteen bit floating point, the setting called W four A sixteen. That is exactly what NNCF's int4 weight compression does, and NNCF even has an AWQ switch. So this paper really explains what that switch does inside.

stops.title: The whole idea
stops.text: The whole paper fits in these two panels. On the left, plain rounding gives every weight a similar rounding error, but that error gets multiplied by the input. So channels that see large activations do the most damage. Keeping those channels in full precision fixes accuracy, but mixed formats are slow. On the right is AWQ's trick. Multiply those weights by a scale before rounding, divide the input by the same scale, and the product is unchanged while their error shrinks. Every weight stays in one simple int4 format.

stops.title: Which weights matter
stops.text: Here is the observation the method is built on. Only about one percent of input channels really matter. The left chart is illustrative, but the bars on the right are real, for OPT six point seven B at three bits. Plain rounding gives a perplexity of 23.54, against 10.86 for the full model. Keep one percent of channels in full precision, chosen by activation size, and it drops to 11.39. Choose them by weight size or at random, and it barely helps. Notice the lesson: look at the activations, not the weights.

stops.title: How the scales are found
stops.text: So how does AWQ pick the scales? Offline, a small generic calibration set runs through the model, and for each layer the average activation size per input channel is measured. The scale is that statistic raised to a power alpha, between zero and one. AWQ tries twenty values of alpha, quantizes, and keeps whichever gives the smallest layer output error. At inference, the inverse scale is folded into the previous operation, such as a layer norm. There is no backpropagation and no weight reconstruction, which is why it needs so little data.

stops.title: Why search at all
stops.text: Why search instead of fixing one scale? Because scaling is not free. In the left chart, the error on the salient weights keeps falling as the scale grows. But a bigger scaled weight can become the maximum of its group of 128, which widens the step size for all its neighbours. That collateral damage keeps rising. On the right, perplexity is best at a scale of two and worse again at four. The alpha search finds this balance automatically, layer by layer.

stops.title: Does it get faster
stops.text: Now the system side. Four times fewer bytes only become speed if the kernel unpacks int4 weights on the fly, and the companion runtime TinyChat does that. On an RTX forty ninety, Llama two seven B goes from 52 to 194 tokens per second, and speed ups reach about 3.9 times. Here is the caveat that matters most for this project. This works because generating one token at a time is memory bound. A video diffusion transformer processes many tokens at once, so expect mostly memory savings and a smaller latency gain.

stops.title: Does accuracy hold
stops.text: And accuracy? This chart shows how much perplexity each method loses at three bits on LLaMA and Llama two, from seven to seventy billion parameters. Shorter bars are better, and AWQ is the shortest in every group, ahead of plain rounding and GPTQ. Look at GPTQ without reordering on LLaMA seven B, losing over three points. The paper also shows AWQ needs about ten times less calibration data than GPTQ and overfits much less when the test domain changes.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So what does the thesis take from it? Call NNCF's compress weights with an int4 mode, group size 128, a calibration dataset, and AWQ switched on. Then check which linear layers it actually matched, because AWQ only applies where a preceding operation can absorb the inverse scale. Calibrate across many denoising timesteps and prompts, since activation sizes change with the noise level. Next, Q-Diffusion shows exactly why that timestep dependence makes quantizing diffusion models harder than language models.
